days.title: The benchmark object, drawn cold
days.full: Pick one object you own with real complexity — a stapler, a shoe, a kettle, a pair of scissors. More than one part, at least one curve. Draw it for fifteen minutes with no technique, no construction, no reference. Just look and draw. Photograph it; this is Day 1 of a series you will finish on Day 365. Then meet the warm-up you will do on every sketch day for the next year: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Put the object somewhere you will still be able to find it in three months.
days.minimum: Draw the benchmark object for ten minutes and photograph it. The warm-up can start tomorrow.
days.question: Before you have learned anything: which part of it do you already expect to get wrong?

days.title: Ghosting, point to point
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then two pages of point-to-point lines. Mark two dots, hover the pen above the paper and rehearse the stroke three or four times, then commit in one movement. No rulers, ever. Lock the wrist and move from the shoulder. A fast wrong line beats a slow tentative one.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: How many rehearsals before the line stops getting better?

days.title: Watch someone else's hand
days.full: Find Spencer Nugent's line and ghosting drills and watch twenty minutes of them with a pen already in your hand. Do not take notes. Copy what he does as he does it, badly, in real time. Pause wherever his hand does something yours does not.
days.minimum: Watch ten minutes. Copy one drill.
days.question: What is his hand doing that yours is not?

days.title: Lines at speed
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then one page of lines drawn deliberately too fast — faster than you can control. Then one page at the speed you would normally use. Then one page somewhere between the two. You are hunting for the speed at which the line stops wobbling but still lands near the mark.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then half a page of lines drawn too fast. Ten minutes.
days.question: At what speed do your lines stop wobbling?

days.title: Line weight
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw the same simple shape — a rectangle with a notch cut out of it — eight times. Change only the line weight each time: heavier on the outer silhouette, lighter on interior detail, heaviest where two forms meet. One shape, eight different readings of it.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the shape twice: once all one weight, once with a heavy silhouette. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which weight makes it look like an object rather than an outline?

days.title: A page that is only lines
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then spend the block filling one large page with nothing but straight lines and arcs — no subject, no object, no meaning. Vary weight, length, spacing and direction. Treat it as a page you would be willing to show someone. Stop when it is full, not when the time is up.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then fifteen minutes on the page. Leave it unfinished and come back to it another day.
days.question: Where on the page did your hand get tired, and can you see it?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. The weekly designer is sitting in the Sunday panel if you want something to look at. Drawing today is allowed but it is not owed.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Long arcs from the shoulder
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then two pages of long sweeping arcs, corner to corner, drawn from the shoulder with the whole arm. Then one page of the same arcs drawn from the wrist. Put the two pages side by side before you stop.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one page of arcs from the shoulder. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which page looks more like it was drawn on purpose?

days.title: Arcs through three points
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then mark three dots on the page and draw a single smooth arc passing through all three. Twenty times, with the dots in different arrangements. When an arc misses, do not correct it — draw the next one beside the failure and leave both.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then five arcs through three points. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is it the start of the arc that goes wrong, or the end?

days.title: Read about what you have been doing
days.full: Read Robertson on line quality and mark-making properly, now that your hand has spent nine days on it. Twenty minutes, pen down. Then write three sentences in the notes about something you have been doing wrong without noticing.
days.minimum: Read for ten minutes. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: What does the book say you are doing that you did not notice you were doing?

days.title: Hatching for tone
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then a strip divided into five boxes, filled with hatching from lightest to darkest. Do it three times: once varying line spacing only, once varying line weight only, once varying both. No shading with the side of the pen.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one five-step strip. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the three ramps reads smoothest from a metre away?

days.title: Cross-hatching
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the same five-step ramp using cross-hatching, changing the angle between layers. Then take the darkest box and try to push it two steps darker without the surface turning to mud.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one cross-hatched ramp. Ten minutes.
days.question: At what point does another layer stop adding darkness and start adding noise?

days.title: One object, lines only
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then pick something on your desk and draw it large, using only the marks from the last two weeks — straight lines, arcs, hatching. No shading, no blending, no outline you have not earned. Fill the block. This is the first time the drills are aimed at a real thing.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then twenty minutes on the object. Stop wherever you are.
days.question: Which marks did you reach for first, and which did you avoid?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Two weeks of line work behind you. If you open the sketchbook today, open it to look rather than to draw.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: The minor axis
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw a straight line and construct twenty ellipses on it, each symmetrical about that line. The minor axis is the short one, and it is the axis that matters — every ellipse you draw for the rest of the year is wrong if this is wrong. Draw the axis first, every time, in a lighter weight.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then eight ellipses on a drawn minor axis. Ten minutes.
days.question: How many can you draw before you stop bothering to draw the axis first?

days.title: Ellipse degree
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then a page of ellipses on one shared minor axis, running from nearly a circle down to nearly a line. Label a few with their rough degree. Then a second page where you try to produce a specific degree on demand — 30, 60, 45 — and check yourself afterwards.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one page running from wide to narrow. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which degree does your hand default to when you are not paying attention?

days.title: Ellipse drills, watched
days.full: Twenty minutes of Nugent's ellipse material with a pen in your hand, copying in real time. This is the drill most beginners skip and most schools test for, so watch how much time he spends on it before he moves on.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, copying one drill.
days.question: How long does he spend on a single ellipse before he accepts it?

days.title: Stacked on a shared axis
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then one long minor axis down the page with eight ellipses stacked along it at even spacing, all the same degree. Then the same again with the degree opening up as they descend, the way a cylinder seen from above behaves.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one stack of five. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which ellipse in the stack is the one that gives the whole thing away?

days.title: Degree change along an axis
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw a long axis and stack ellipses along it where the degree changes progressively — a cone rather than a cylinder. Do it three times at three different rates of change. Then once deliberately wrong, with the degree changing the opposite way.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one correct stack and one deliberately wrong one. Ten minutes.
days.question: What object does the wrong one look like?

days.title: Something round, drawn properly
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then find an object built from circles — a roll of tape, a mug, a tin, a bottle — and draw it four times from four angles, constructing every ellipse on a drawn minor axis. Keep the construction visible. Do not clean it up.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the object once, with the axis drawn. Twenty minutes.
days.question: Which of the four angles was hardest, and why that one?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Optional, and genuinely so.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Tilted in space
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then ellipses whose minor axis is neither vertical nor horizontal — tilted at every angle across the page, like coins dropped on a table and caught mid-fall. Twenty of them. The axis still gets drawn first.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then ten tilted ellipses with axes drawn. Ten minutes.
days.question: Does turning the paper help, or does it cheat you out of the drill?

days.title: Ellipses lying on a plane
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw a horizon line and scatter twelve ellipses across the page as though they were circles lying flat on the ground — nearer ones more open, further ones narrower, all with vertical minor axes. Then the same again with them standing upright instead.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then six flat-lying ellipses under a horizon line. Ten minutes.
days.question: Where does the horizon have to be for an ellipse to close into a line?

days.title: Ellipses at speed
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then fill a page with ellipses drawn in about two seconds each — no axis drawn, no corrections, no second passes. Then a second page at your careful speed. Look at both from across the room before you decide which is better.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one fast page. Ten minutes.
days.question: From across the room, can you tell which page was the careful one?

days.title: Read the ellipse section
days.full: Read the front sections of Eissen and Steur properly. Twenty minutes, pen down. Find what they say about ellipses and set it against what you have actually been doing for the last ten days. Three sentences in the notes on the difference.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: Is your problem the shape of the ellipse, or the axis it sits on?

days.title: Lines and ellipses, together
days.full: No new material today. Warm-up, then one page that needs both: a grid of straight lines with an ellipse inscribed in every cell. Twenty cells. Each ellipse has to touch all four sides of its cell. This is the first time the two drills have to cooperate.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then six cells. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the two is holding the other back right now?

days.title: Four objects, one page
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then four round objects from your kitchen on a single page, drawn at the same scale, each with its construction left visible. Arrange them as one group rather than four separate drawings. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two of the four. Twenty minutes.
days.question: Do they look like they are sitting on the same table?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Four weeks in. Nothing is owed today.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Boxes in one-point
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then a horizon line, a single vanishing point, and twenty freehand boxes — above the horizon, below it, left and right of the point. No rulers. Let the lines overshoot the corners rather than stopping short.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then eight boxes on one vanishing point. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which boxes look wrong, and are they the ones nearest the vanishing point?

days.title: Boxes in two-point
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then two vanishing points placed further apart than feels necessary, and fifteen boxes between them. Then five more with the points deliberately close together, so you can see the distortion you are trying to avoid.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then six boxes on two points. Ten minutes.
days.question: How close can the two points get before the box stops looking like an object?

days.title: Perspective, watched slowly
days.full: Twenty minutes of The Design Sketchbook on freehand perspective, drawing along as it plays. Chung moves slower than Robertson reads, which is the point of today.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, drawing along.
days.question: What does he draw before he draws the box?

days.title: Box grids
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then build a grid of boxes sharing vanishing points — stacked and aligned, like a shelf of identical cartons. Twelve at minimum. When one goes wrong, leave it and build the next off a neighbour that is right.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then four boxes sharing both vanishing points. Ten minutes.
days.question: When one box goes wrong, does the next one inherit the error?

days.title: One box, rotated
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the same box drawn eight times, rotating a little further each time as if it were turning on a turntable. Keep the size and the eye level constant so rotation is the only thing changing.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the box three times at three rotations. Ten minutes.
days.question: At which rotation does it stop reading as a box?

days.title: A boxy thing, constructed
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then find something essentially rectangular — a book, a router, a toaster, a speaker — and construct it inside a drawn box in two-point perspective. Build the box first, then cut the object out of it. Keep every construction line. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the enclosing box and a rough object inside it. Twenty minutes.
days.question: Did you build the box honestly, or draw the object and put a box around it afterwards?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Subdividing a plane
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw a plane in perspective and divide it into halves, quarters and eighths using diagonals, with no measuring. Then into thirds, which is harder and worth the struggle. Six planes at six angles.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one plane divided into quarters. Ten minutes.
days.question: Why does the far half come out smaller than you expect it to?

days.title: True centre, the X method
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then use crossed diagonals to find the true centre of planes in perspective, and use that centre to place something — a door in a wall, a button on a panel, a hole in a lid. Ten planes, each with something placed centrally on it.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then four planes with their true centre marked. Ten minutes.
days.question: How far off was your eyeballed centre before you checked it?

days.title: Extending and mirroring
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then take a box and extend it — double its length in perspective using diagonals, then double it again. Then mirror a form across a plane so the reflection is correctly foreshortened. Six of each.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one box doubled in length. Ten minutes.
days.question: Does the second doubling look half the size of the first, and should it?

days.title: Read the perspective chapter
days.full: Read Robertson on basic perspective properly. Twenty minutes, pen down. You have ten days of boxes behind you, so read it as a correction rather than an introduction. Three sentences in the notes.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: Which of your habits does the chapter quietly contradict?

days.title: The same box, four eye levels
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then one box drawn four times: far above the horizon, just above, just below, far below. Same box, same rotation — only the eye level moves. Then draw what it would be at eye level exactly.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the box once above and once below the horizon. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which eye level makes it look most like a product photograph?

days.title: Five boxes, one space
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then a single scene: five rectangular objects of different sizes on one surface, sharing one horizon and one pair of vanishing points. They have to look like they belong in the same room. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two objects sharing a horizon. Twenty minutes.
days.question: Which object betrays that it was drawn separately from the others?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Light week starts tomorrow — nothing new until day 50.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Spread out six weeks
days.full: Light week. Nothing new until day 50. Lay out everything you have drawn since day 1, in order, on the floor if you need the space. Photograph the spread. Find three things that are visibly better and one thing that has not moved at all.
days.minimum: Lay it out and photograph it. Five minutes.
days.question: What improved without you trying to improve it?

days.title: Redraw day two
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then redraw the day 2 ghosting page exactly as it was set — two pages of point-to-point lines. Put the old page next to the new one when you are done.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is the difference in the lines, or in how long you hesitate before each one?

days.title: Redraw an ellipse page
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then find your worst ellipse page from days 15 to 28 and draw it again on fresh paper. Do not look at the old one while you work.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Did you fix it, or did you avoid the part that was hard?

days.title: Rewatch something
days.full: Light week. Pick a video you already watched in the last six weeks and watch it again, pausing every time he does something you now understand. Nothing new today.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of it.
days.question: What did you not notice the first time?

days.title: Redraw a box page
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then the same again with a box page from days 29 to 42. Fresh paper, old page face down until you have finished.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which page did you pick, and was it really the worst one?

days.title: Finish something unfinished
days.full: Light week, short block. Find a page you abandoned and finish it. If nothing is unfinished, take the page you like most and push it twenty minutes further than you wanted to.
days.minimum: Fifteen minutes on it, then stop.
days.question: Why did you stop the first time?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. New material starts again tomorrow.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Cylinders, built in boxes
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then construct cylinders the long way: draw the box first, find the centre of each end face with the X method, inscribe the ellipse, connect the sides. Eight cylinders at eight orientations. Every one starts as a box. Then draw one by eye for comparison.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two cylinders built from boxes. Ten minutes.
days.question: How much faster was the eyeballed one, and how much worse?

days.title: Cylinders lying down
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then cylinders that are not vertical — lying on a surface, leaning, pointing towards you. Twelve of them. Foreshortening a cylinder along its own axis is the case everyone gets wrong, so spend the time there rather than on the easy ones.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then three cylinders, one pointing towards you. Ten minutes.
days.question: What happens to the near ellipse as the cylinder turns to face you?

days.title: Cylinder construction, watched
days.full: Twenty minutes on cylinder and cone construction, drawing along. Watch specifically for what happens when the construction goes wrong mid-drawing — that is the part tutorials usually edit out.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, drawing along.
days.question: When it goes wrong, does he fix it or draw over it?

days.title: Cones
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then cones: the base ellipse, the axis perpendicular to it, the apex on that axis, the sides tangent to the ellipse. Ten cones at varied angles. Then four truncated cones, which are most of the real objects you will ever draw.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then three cones with the axis drawn. Ten minutes.
days.question: Where exactly do the sides meet the base ellipse — and is it where you drew them?

days.title: Spheres
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then spheres, which are easy to draw and hard to place. Draw eight circles, then give each an equator and a meridian in perspective so it reads as a ball rather than a disc. Then sit each one on a surface with a contact shadow.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then three spheres with an equator drawn. Ten minutes.
days.question: What makes a circle become a sphere — the lines on it, or the shadow under it?

days.title: An object, in primitives only
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then pick something moderately complex — a hairdryer, a kettle, a power drill — and draw it as nothing but boxes, cylinders, cones and spheres. No detail, no surface, no attempt to make it look good. You are looking for the solids underneath. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then block the object in with three primitives. Twenty minutes.
days.question: Which primitive did you have to invent because none of the four quite fit?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Four days of Phase 1 left.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Cutting through
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then take a cylinder and cut it with a plane — vertical, horizontal, diagonal — and draw the section the cut reveals. Then the same for a cone, where the sections are the interesting ones. Six cuts in total.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one cylinder cut vertically and one diagonally. Ten minutes.
days.question: The diagonal cut through the cylinder — is that an ellipse, or something else?

days.title: Crude assemblies
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then invent rather than observe: stack and intersect primitives into things that could be products but are not. Six of them, about thirty seconds of thought each. Ugly is required, not tolerated.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two invented assemblies. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the six would you be embarrassed to show, and what does it have that the others do not?

days.title: The same assemblies, again
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then take the two least embarrassing assemblies from yesterday and draw each one twice more, from different angles. This is the first time you are drawing something that exists only in your head from more than one direction.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one assembly from a second angle. Ten minutes.
days.question: Did the object stay the same shape when you turned it?

days.title: Phase 1, looked at properly
days.full: No new material. Lay out days 1 to 59 in order. Write three things in the notes: the drill that improved most, the drill you have been avoiding, and one thing your hand still cannot do. Then spend ten minutes on whichever you named as avoided. Do not redraw the benchmark object — that waits for day 90.
days.minimum: Lay it out and write the three answers. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the three was hardest to write down?

days.title: Addition
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then build forms by adding: start with one box and attach a second, then a cylinder, then a wedge. Eight assemblies. Every joint has to be believable — where two forms meet, the intersection line is the drawing.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Where two forms meet, did you draw the intersection or just stop the lines?

days.title: A remote control, taken apart
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then a TV remote — yours, in your hand, not from memory. Draw it three times: once as the primitive stack underneath it, once as the real object, once exploded with the parts pulled apart along one axis. All three on one sheet. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the primitive stack only. Twenty minutes.
days.question: How many primitives did it actually take, and was it fewer than you expected?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Phase 2 has started; nothing is owed today.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Subtraction
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then cut into forms rather than adding to them: a box with a channel milled through it, a cylinder with a slot, a block with a pocket. Eight subtractions. Draw the hidden edges of each cut in a lighter weight so the removed volume is visible.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Can you tell from the drawing how deep the cut goes?

days.title: Intersection
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the third boolean: two forms overlapping, keeping only the shared volume. A cylinder through a box, a sphere through a wedge. Six of them. This is the one that forces you to think in three dimensions rather than two.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Could you predict the intersection curve before you drew it?

days.title: A product, taken apart on screen
days.full: Twenty minutes of Nugent's form-building and product-teardown material, drawing along. Watch how he decides which primitive to start with — that first decision does most of the work.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, drawing along.
days.question: Which primitive does he reach for first, and why that one?

days.title: A charger, as a stack
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then a plug-in charger, the brick kind. Primitives first, then resolved. Four angles on one page. It is a nearly featureless object, which is the point — there is nowhere to hide a proportion error.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the charger from two angles. Ten minutes.
days.question: With no detail to distract you, where does the drawing go wrong?

days.title: A speaker, as a stack
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then a Bluetooth speaker, or anything with a soft rectangular body and a grille. Primitive stack, then resolved, then one view where you draw the parting line and the grille and nothing else at all.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the primitive stack. Ten minutes.
days.question: How much can you remove before it stops being that object?

days.title: One object, three constructions
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then pick one object and build it three different ways: as an additive stack, as a subtracted block, and as a single form with details laid on top. Same object, three logics. Fill the block, then write in the notes which was fastest and which was truest.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two of the three constructions. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Which construction was fastest, and which was truest?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: The space around it
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw four objects by their negative space only — the gap under a chair, between a handle and a body, inside a loop. Then draw the object itself and see whether the gap you drew actually fits it.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two objects drawn as negative space. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is the gap the shape you thought it was?

days.title: Ellipses and boxes, still
days.full: Resurfacing drill, no new material. Warm-up, then a page of boxes in two-point with an ellipse inscribed on three faces of each. Fundamentals do not retire when a phase ends.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then four boxes with inscribed ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which has decayed more in six weeks — the boxes or the ellipses?

days.title: Assemblies with intent
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then invent three objects that could exist — a thing that clamps, a thing that pours, a thing that plugs in — using only the three booleans. No styling, no detail. The boolean is the idea.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one invented object. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the three booleans did you avoid?

days.title: Simplifying shape
days.full: Read Eissen and Steur on simplifying shape and elementary geometric shapes. Twenty minutes, pen down. You have spent two weeks doing this by instinct — read it as a correction. Three sentences in the notes.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: What do they simplify away that you have been keeping?

resource.section: simplifying shape and elementary geometric shapes

days.title: Small radii
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then take a plain box and put a small radius on every edge. Draw it four times at four radius sizes, from barely there to obvious. A radius is drawn with two lines and a highlight, never one soft line — that is the whole trick.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the box at two radii. Ten minutes.
days.question: At what radius does the box stop looking machined and start looking moulded?

days.title: The same object, three radii
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then one object drawn three times, identical except for corner treatment: sharp, small radius, large soft radius. Same silhouette, same size, same angle, in a row. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two of the three. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Which of the three looks more expensive, and can you say why?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Large radii and soft forms
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then push the radius until the box is nearly a pillow and the flat faces have almost vanished. Six forms along that range. Find the point where you can no longer tell it began as a box.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then three forms along the range. Ten minutes.
days.question: Where exactly did it stop being a box?

days.title: Variable radius
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then edges whose radius changes along their length — tight at one end, generous at the other. This is what most real products have and almost no beginner draws. Six edges, each with a cross-section drawn beside it at three points along the edge.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one variable-radius edge with two sections. Ten minutes.
days.question: Does the highlight along the edge change width the way it should?

days.title: Corners, watched
days.full: Twenty minutes on drawing radii, fillets and soft edges, drawing along. Watch specifically how the highlight is handled — that is what makes a radius read as a radius rather than a smudge.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, drawing along.
days.question: How many marks does it take him to make an edge look soft?

days.title: Parting lines
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw six moulded objects and put an honest parting line on each — where the two halves of the tool would meet — and follow it all the way around the form. If you cannot decide where it goes, the form cannot be moulded as drawn.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two objects with a parting line taken all the way round. Ten minutes.
days.question: Where does your parting line have to go, and does the form allow it?

days.title: Draft
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then redraw three of yesterday's objects with visible draft — faces tilted a degree or two so the part can leave the tool. Exaggerate it until you can see it, then dial it back to where it is just believable.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one object with exaggerated draft. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which way does each face have to lean, and what does that tell you about the tool?

days.title: A part that could actually be made
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then design and draw one moulded part — a housing, a cap, a handle — obeying everything from this block: consistent wall, real radii, a parting line that goes all the way round, draft in one direction. Draw it, then draw its cross-section. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the part and a rough cross-section. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Your engineering brain knows this is wrong somewhere. Where?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Shutlines and gaps
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the line where two parts meet: consistent gap, aligned radii on both sides, and the shadow that falls into it. Six shutlines on six forms. Drawn as a single line it reads as a scratch; drawn as a gap it reads as an assembly.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two shutlines drawn as gaps. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is your gap the same width all the way along, and should it be?

days.title: Perspective, still
days.full: Resurfacing drill, no new material. Warm-up, then a page of boxes in two-point at four eye levels, subdivided with the X method. Twenty minutes on Phase 1 material.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then four boxes with true centres found. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is the X method faster now, or are you still avoiding it?

days.title: One part, the whole vocabulary
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then one object carrying everything from this block at once — two sizes of radius, a parting line, visible draft, one shutline. Draw it large. This is the drawing you show someone when they ask what you have been doing.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the object with radii and a parting line only. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the five did you fudge?

days.title: How the part is actually made
days.full: Read a narrow section of Thompson on injection moulding — draft, wall thickness, parting lines. Twenty minutes, pen down. This is a reference book, not a book to read through: find the four pages that match what you drew this fortnight and stop there. Three sentences in the notes.
days.minimum: Ten minutes. Find one thing you drew wrong.
days.question: What did you draw this fortnight that could not be manufactured?

days.title: Spread out Phase 2
days.full: Light week. Nothing new until day 96. Lay out days 61 to 88 in order. Find the corner treatment drawing you would be least embarrassed to show, and put it somewhere you will see it.
days.minimum: Lay it out. Five minutes.
days.question: What changed between the first boolean drawing and the last?

days.title: The benchmark object, ninety days on
days.full: Light week, and the first redraw. Find the object you drew on Day 1. Same conditions exactly: fifteen minutes, cold, no construction, no reference, no technique you would not have had on Day 1. Photograph it. Then — only then — put the two drawings side by side.
days.minimum: Fifteen minutes on the object, photographed. The comparison can wait until tomorrow.
days.question: What did you expect to have improved, and is that what actually improved?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Two drawings of the same object, ninety days apart, are now sitting in the log.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Redraw a boolean page
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then redraw your worst page from days 61 to 74. Fresh paper, old page face down.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Did you pick the worst one, or the easiest one to fix?

days.title: Redraw a corner page
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then the same with a page from the corner treatment block — but this time draw the cross-section first and the object second.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Does leading with the section make the corner easier?

days.title: Rewatch a form video
days.full: Light week. Rewatch something from the last four weeks, pausing wherever you now understand what he is doing. Nothing new.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of it.
days.question: What was invisible to you a month ago?

days.title: What the two drawings say
days.full: Light week, last day. Put the Day 1 and Day 90 benchmark drawings side by side properly and write in the notes: what is better, what is the same, and what got worse. Something usually gets worse — people draw slower and more carefully as they learn and lose the looseness. Name it if you see it.
days.minimum: Write the three answers. Ten minutes.
days.question: What got worse?

days.title: Five objects, measured by eye
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then five objects from your desk, drawn from life, no photographs. Before each one, hold the pen at arm's length and measure the object's height against its width. Write the ratio on the page. Then draw it, then check.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two objects with their ratios written down. Ten minutes.
days.question: How far off was your guess before you measured?

days.title: The desk, as one drawing
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then your actual desk, as it is, without tidying it first. Everything on it, in one drawing, sharing one perspective. Harder than five separate objects, and that is the point — things have to relate to each other. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then three objects on the desk, correctly related. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Which object did you move without meaning to?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Ellipses, still
days.full: Resurfacing drill, no new material. Warm-up, then twenty minutes of ellipses on drawn minor axes at varied degrees, then six cylinders built inside boxes. Phase 1 material, twelve weeks on.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two cylinders built in boxes. Ten minutes.
days.question: Are you still drawing the minor axis first?

days.title: Sighting and proportion
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then one object drawn three times: once by eye with no measuring, once with every proportion sighted and marked before a line goes down, once by eye again afterwards. The third drawing is the one that matters.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the object by eye and then sighted. Ten minutes.
days.question: Did measuring once change what your eye does afterwards?

days.title: Cross-sections
days.full: Read Eissen and Steur on cross-sections. Twenty minutes, pen down. You have been drawing objects from the outside; this is about what is going on inside them. Three sentences in the notes.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: Which object on your desk do you not understand the section of?

days.title: Five from the kitchen
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then five kitchen objects from life. Kitchens are good for this because the objects are honest — handles that have to be held, spouts that have to pour. Sight every proportion before you draw it.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two kitchen objects, sighted. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which one is shaped by the hand and which by the manufacturing?

days.title: The same object, five times, faster each time
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then one object drawn five times: ten minutes, five, three, two, one. Same object, same angle. Decide before each drawing what you will keep and what you will drop.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the object at three minutes and at one. Ten minutes.
days.question: At one minute, what did you keep?

days.title: Five objects, one space
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then five objects from life arranged as a group and drawn as one scene, with one horizon and consistent scale. Not five drawings on a page — one drawing containing five things. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then three objects sharing one horizon. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Do they cast their shadows in the same direction?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Cross-contours
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw contour lines across simple forms — a cylinder, a box with a radius, a sphere — as though a wire were wrapped around the surface. Six forms, contours in both directions. The contour has to sit on the surface, not float above it.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two forms with contours in both directions. Ten minutes.
days.question: Do the contours meet the silhouette at right angles, and should they?

days.title: Contours on compound curves
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the same on forms that curve two ways at once — a computer mouse, a bar of soap, a helmet. Draw the contours first and the silhouette last, which is backwards from how you will want to do it.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one compound form, contours before silhouette. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is the silhouette easier or harder once the contours are down?

days.title: Tangency
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the join between a flat face and a curve, done two ways: once where the curve meets the flat abruptly, once where it runs in tangentially. Six pairs. The difference is small on paper and enormous on a real product.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two pairs. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the two reads as cheaper, and is that always true?

days.title: Surface flow, watched
days.full: Twenty minutes of the Domestika concept sketching course, drawing along. Start it now — it runs analog to digital and you will still be using it in Phase 3. Watch for how surfaces are made to flow into one another.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of it.
days.question: Where does one surface end and the next begin?

days.title: Boxes and cylinders, still
days.full: Resurfacing drill, no new material. Warm-up, then boxes in two-point at four eye levels, then cylinders lying at angles. Twenty minutes of Phase 1.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then four boxes and two cylinders. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which Phase 1 drill is automatic now, and which still needs thinking about?

days.title: A speed form
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then a speed form: a shape with no function at all, judged only on whether the surfaces flow. Draw it from four angles with cross-contours on every one. It has to be the same object in all four. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the form from two angles. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Is it the same object in all four drawings, honestly?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Compound curves, from life
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then find the most organically shaped object you own — a shoe, a kettle, a mouse, a bottle — and draw it with cross-contours from three angles. This is the hardest observational drawing you have done.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the object from one angle with contours. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which part of it could you not describe with contours?

days.title: Silhouette only
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then twelve objects drawn as flat black silhouettes, no interior detail at all. Then cover the page, wait a minute, and try to name them. A form that fails as a silhouette fails.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then six silhouettes. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which ones could you still name?

days.title: Stance
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the same object drawn six times with different stance — leaning forward, sitting back, planted, poised, heavy, light. Nothing changes but the attitude. This is the vocabulary designers actually argue about.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the object in two stances. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which stance would you defend in a meeting?

days.title: Twenty on one page
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then twenty variants of one form on a single page, none bigger than a matchbox. Twenty, not twelve. The last five are the ones worth having, which is the only reason the first fifteen exist.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then ten variants. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the twenty did you not expect to draw?

days.title: The brief
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then your first real design prompt: pick a familiar object you own and redesign it. Write the brief in one sentence in the notes first — what is actually wrong with the one you have. Then start thumbnails. No rendering, no detail, nothing bigger than a matchbox.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then write the one-sentence brief and draw five thumbnails. Ten minutes.
days.question: What is actually wrong with the one you own?

days.title: Thirty thumbnails
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then get to thirty thumbnails of the redesign. Thirty is the number, not a target to approach. When you run out of ideas at eighteen, that is where the work starts. At the end circle three — not your favourites, the three most different from each other. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then fifteen thumbnails. Thirty minutes.
days.question: At which number did you run out, and what came after that?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Phase 2 ends tomorrow.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Phase 2, looked at properly
days.full: No new material. Lay out days 61 to 118. Write in the notes: the drawing where primitives finally clicked, the corner treatment you still cannot draw, and which of your three circled thumbnails you would take into Phase 3. Then spend ten minutes redrawing the corner you named.
days.minimum: Lay it out and write the three answers. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which thumbnail did you circle because it was good, and which because it was safe?

days.title: Where is the light coming from
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then one simple form drawn six times, with the light source in a different place each time and marked on the page with an arrow. Nothing else changes. Before you shade anything, decide where the light is and write it down — most bad rendering is a light source that moved halfway through.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the form lit from two directions, arrows marked. Ten minutes.
days.question: When you shade without deciding first, where does your hand assume the light is?

days.title: Light logic
days.full: Read Robertson on light logic. Twenty minutes, pen down. This is the chapter that makes the rest of the phase possible, so read it properly rather than skimming to the pictures. Three sentences in the notes.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: What is the difference between a shadow and a dark side, and did you know it before today?

days.title: Terminator and core shadow
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then spheres and cylinders with the terminator drawn deliberately — the line where the form turns away from the light — and the core shadow sitting just inside it. Eight forms. The core shadow is darker than the cast shadow, which is the opposite of what most people assume.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two forms with the terminator and core shadow marked. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is your core shadow darker than your cast shadow, and can you defend that?

days.title: Reflected light
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the same forms again, now with light bouncing back into the shadow side from the surface underneath. The shadow side is never one flat tone. Six forms, each sitting on a different-coloured surface — white paper, dark table, mid grey.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one form with bounce from a light surface and one from a dark. Ten minutes.
days.question: How much bounce is too much before the form stops reading as solid?

days.title: Cast shadows, constructed
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then stop guessing at shadows and construct them: light source, rays through the silhouette edges, intersection with the ground plane. Do it for a box, a cylinder and a cone. Then cast one shadow up a wall. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one constructed box shadow on the ground. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: How far off was the shadow you would have drawn by eye?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Phase 3 has started.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Occlusion
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the dark line where two surfaces meet and light cannot get in — under a button, along a shutline, where a leg meets the floor. Six objects, occlusion only, no other shading at all. It is a small mark that does most of the work.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two objects with occlusion only. Ten minutes.
days.question: How much of the form can you describe with nothing but the darkest lines?

days.title: Three values
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then six objects rendered in exactly three values — light, mid, dark — with no blending and no fourth tone. Decide which plane gets which value before you start. Anything you cannot say in three values you do not yet understand.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two objects in three values. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which plane did you want a fourth value for?

days.title: Five values
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the same objects in five values: highlight, light, mid, core shadow, reflected light. Now the cast shadow gets its own value too. Six objects. Keep the five steps genuinely distinct — if two of them read the same, you have four.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one object in five values. Ten minutes.
days.question: Do all five read as distinct from across the room, or do two collapse?

days.title: Value, watched
days.full: Twenty minutes of marker and value rendering, drawing along. Watch the order of operations — which value goes down first, and what is left as paper.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, drawing along.
days.question: What does he leave as bare paper, and for how long?

days.title: Matte plastic
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then matte plastic, the default material of everything you own. Soft gradient from light to dark, a broad diffuse highlight with no sharp edge, and almost no reflection of the surroundings. Four objects. This is the baseline every other material is a deviation from.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one object in matte plastic. Ten minutes.
days.question: What makes it read as plastic rather than as plaster?

days.title: Gloss plastic
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the same form in gloss: a hard-edged highlight, a compressed gradient, and a dark reflection of whatever is around it. Draw one object matte and the same object gloss, side by side, same light. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the form in gloss only. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Which one took longer, and which one is more convincing?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Rubber
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then rubber and soft-touch: a highlight that is present but broken, edges that read soft even when the form is sharp, and a slightly dusty surface. Four objects — a grip, a foot, a seal, a wheel.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one rubber object. Ten minutes.
days.question: How do you make an edge look soft without rounding it?

days.title: Brushed aluminium
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then brushed metal: directional streaking that follows the brushing, a highlight smeared along that direction, and a dark band where the surface turns. Four objects. Get the brush direction wrong and it reads as dirt.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one brushed panel with the grain running correctly. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which way is the grain running, and why that way on a real part?

days.title: Metals, watched
days.full: Twenty minutes on rendering metal — brushed, polished, chrome — drawing along. Metal is almost entirely the reflection of its surroundings, so watch what he decides those surroundings are.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, drawing along.
days.question: What environment is he reflecting, and did he ever say so?

days.title: Chrome
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then chrome, which is not a material so much as a mirror. A dark band for the ground, a light band for the sky, a hard horizon between them wrapped around the form. Four objects. No mid-tones, no gradient, no mercy.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one chrome form with a horizon wrapped around it. Ten minutes.
days.question: Where is the horizon on the object, and what decides that?

days.title: Glass
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then glass: the far wall of the object is visible through the near wall, it is darkest at the edges and lightest in the middle, and it bends whatever is behind it. Four objects. Draw what is behind the glass first, then distort it.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one glass object with the far wall visible. Ten minutes.
days.question: Did you draw the thickness of the glass, or only its surface?

days.title: One form, four materials
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then anodised finish — the flat, slightly powdery metal of a laptop body — and then the point of the fortnight: one single form drawn four times in four materials, same light, same angle. Matte, gloss, metal, rubber. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the form in two materials. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Which material changed the form's character most, and would you have predicted that?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Fabric and wood
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the two that behave least like the others. Fabric: no highlight to speak of, form described entirely by folds and by the soft edge of the silhouette. Wood: grain that follows the form and gets denser as the surface turns away. Two objects each.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one fabric object and one wooden one. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the two is harder, and is it the one you expected?

days.title: Spread out Phase 3
days.full: Light week. Nothing new until day 149. Lay out days 121 to 141 in order. Put the three-value studies next to the five-value studies and look at what the extra two values actually bought you.
days.minimum: Lay it out. Five minutes.
days.question: Did five values say more than three, or just take longer?

days.title: Redraw a value study
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then pick your least convincing value study and draw it again — same object, same light, no new technique. Old page face down.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Was it the values that were wrong, or the light source moving?

days.title: Rewatch a rendering video
days.full: Light week. Rewatch a rendering video from this phase, pausing wherever he does something you attempted and could not do. Nothing new.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of it.
days.question: What did he do quickly that took you twenty minutes?

days.title: Redraw a material
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then redraw whichever material defeated you — chrome, glass, fabric, whichever it was. Same form as before so the comparison is honest.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Did knowing it defeated you once make it easier or harder to start?

days.title: Finish a rendering
days.full: Light week, short block. Find a rendering you abandoned halfway and finish it. If nothing is unfinished, take the material study you like most and push it twenty minutes further.
days.minimum: Fifteen minutes on it, then stop.
days.question: At what point does a rendering stop improving?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: What the value studies say
days.full: Light week, last day. Line up every material study from days 131 to 141 and sort them best to worst. Write in the notes which three you can now draw reliably and which three you cannot. Marker starts tomorrow.
days.minimum: Sort them and name three of each. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which material do you avoid choosing when you get to pick?

days.title: Marker layering
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then markers, starting with the only rule that matters: work light to dark, and every pass makes it darker permanently. One page of flat swatches, one page of two-layer swatches, one page of three. Learn what the third layer costs.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one page of layered swatches. Ten minutes.
days.question: How many layers before the paper gives up?

days.title: Markers, watched
days.full: Twenty minutes of marker technique, drawing along with markers actually in your hand. Watch the speed — marker work fails slow and succeeds fast, which is the opposite of pencil.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, drawing along.
days.question: How fast is he actually moving, and what happens when he hesitates?

days.title: Blending
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then blending: two markers of neighbouring value worked into each other while both are still wet, and the same join made after the first has dried. Six pairs. One of these works and one does not, and you need to feel the difference.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then three blended pairs. Ten minutes.
days.question: How long do you actually have before the edge sets?

days.title: Underlays
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then underlays: a loose grey marker base laid down first, describing only the big value structure, with the drawing built on top of it. Four objects. The underlay should look like nothing on its own.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one underlay and the drawing on top. Ten minutes.
days.question: Can you still see the underlay in the finished drawing, and should you be able to?

days.title: Light to dark, all the way
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then one object taken from blank paper to finished marker rendering in the correct order: lightest value everywhere, then mids, then darks, then the pen line, then the highlight last. Photograph it at each stage. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the object to the mid-value stage. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: At which stage did it look best, and did you keep going anyway?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Marker and line together
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the relationship between the marker and the pen line: line first then marker, marker first then line, and one with almost no line at all. Same object three times. The third one is the hardest and usually the best.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the object with line-first and marker-first. Ten minutes.
days.question: How little line can the drawing survive on?

days.title: Ellipses and perspective, still
days.full: Resurfacing drill, no new material. Warm-up, then twenty minutes of Phase 1: cylinders built in boxes at four orientations, and one page of ellipses at varied degrees. Twenty-two weeks in.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two cylinders built in boxes. Ten minutes.
days.question: Has rendering made your construction sloppier?

days.title: Knowing when to stop
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then four renderings of four objects, and for each one decide in advance how many minutes it gets: five, ten, fifteen, twenty. Stop at the buzzer with the drawing wherever it is. Then look at all four and pick the best.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the five-minute one and the fifteen-minute one. Ten minutes.
days.question: Was the best one the one that got the most time?

days.title: Surface, texture, light and ambiance
days.full: Read Eissen and Steur on surface and texture, and on light, ambiance and surroundings. Twenty minutes, pen down. You have spent four weeks making surfaces; this is about the room they sit in. Three sentences in the notes.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: What is your default background, and what is it doing to every object you draw?

resource.section: surface and texture, light and ambiance

days.title: Layers and masking
days.full: No warm-up on paper today — do it on the screen instead, with the same two pages. Then set up a digital file properly: line layer, base value layer, shadow layer, highlight layer, each masked to the silhouette. Render one simple object with every stage on its own layer.
days.minimum: Set up the layer stack and block in the base value. Ten minutes.
days.question: What can you now undo that you could not on paper, and is that always good?

days.title: A Phase 2 sketch, rendered
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then take one of your Phase 2 drawings — a corner-treatment study or a speed form — scan or photograph it, and render it digitally over the top. The drawing is already done; today is only about value and material. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the scan cleaned up and a base value laid in. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Did the old drawing hold up under rendering, or did its errors surface?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Gradients, digitally
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the digital versions of everything from the materials fortnight: soft gradient, hard highlight, chrome horizon, brushed streaking. Four swatches, each one matching an analog study you already made. Put them side by side.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two digital swatches matched to analog ones. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which reads as more convincing, and which took less time?

days.title: Cleaning up a scan
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the unglamorous skill: photograph a pencil sketch under bad light and get it to a clean, high-contrast line drawing on a white ground. Levels, not erasing. Do three. Portfolios live or die on this and nobody teaches it.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one sketch cleaned up. Ten minutes.
days.question: How much of the original pencil texture is worth keeping?

days.title: Analog under, digital over
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the workflow you will probably keep: loose marker underlay on paper, scanned, finished digitally. One object all the way through. The point is that neither half has to be perfect.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the marker underlay only, scanned. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which half of the process do you enjoy more, and which produces the better drawing?

days.title: Digital, watched
days.full: Twenty minutes of the Domestika course's digital modules, working along in your own file. You started this course in Phase 2 — pick it up where you left it rather than starting again.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of it.
days.question: What is he doing in two clicks that you were doing in twenty?

days.title: Analog against digital
days.full: No new material. Put your best analog rendering and your best digital rendering side by side and write in the notes which one a reviewer would spend longer looking at, and why. Then note which one you would rather have spent the afternoon making.
days.minimum: Put them side by side and write the two answers. Ten minutes.
days.question: If they disagree — the better drawing and the better afternoon — which one should win?

days.title: Project 1 — the brief
days.full: Project 1 starts. Pick a simple object with few parts: a desk lamp, a hand tool, a water bottle. Modest scope is deliberate — the point is completing a full loop, not ambition. Write the brief: who it is for, what is wrong with the current ones, and one constraint you are imposing on yourself. Then begin thumbnails. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Write the brief and draw ten thumbnails. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: What constraint did you choose, and is it one that will actually bite?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Project 1 is under way.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Project 1 — fifty thumbnails
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then get the thumbnail count to fifty. You did thirty on day 118, so you know what happens after twenty-five. Nothing bigger than a matchbox, no rendering, no detail.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then fifteen more thumbnails. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which thumbnail did you draw twice without noticing?

days.title: Project 1 — three directions
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then choose three directions from the fifty and draw each one properly at a decent size, three views each. Choose for difference, not for quality. One of them should make you slightly uncomfortable.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two of the three directions at one view each. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which one makes you uncomfortable, and is that because it is bad or because it is unfamiliar?

days.title: How this gets presented
days.full: Read Eissen and Steur, Product Design Presentation, on how process work is laid out on a page. Twenty minutes, pen down. You will be building an eight to ten page document at the end of this week, so read it as preparation rather than theory. Three sentences in the notes.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: How much of a page is normally given to the thing that was rejected?

days.title: Project 1 — refine one
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then kill two of the three and refine the survivor. Proportion, corner treatment, parting line, stance — everything from Phase 2 applied to your own object rather than someone else's. Draw it from four angles.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the chosen direction from two angles. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which one did you kill that you are not sure about?

days.title: Project 1 — orthographic views
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then front, side, top and one section, drawn flat and consistent, with overall dimensions marked by eye. This is the drawing that proves the object could exist. Your engineering background should make this the easiest day of the week.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then front and side views. Ten minutes.
days.question: Do the three views actually agree with each other?

days.title: Project 1 — the final rendering
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the hero rendering: one three-quarter view, one light source decided in advance, materials chosen deliberately, taken all the way to a finish. Everything from days 121 to 166 lands here. Fill the block and do not start over.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the rendering to the mid-value stage. Thirty minutes.
days.question: Which material decision are you making for the drawing rather than for the object?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Project 1 — finishing the rendering
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then finish it: darks, occlusion, highlight last, and a background that is doing something rather than nothing. Stop when it is done, using whatever you learned on day 157 about when that is.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the darks and the highlight. Ten minutes.
days.question: Did you stop at the right point this time?

days.title: Project 1 — the first four pages
days.full: No warm-up needed today. Lay out the first four pages of the process document: the brief, the thumbnails, the three directions, and why you killed two of them. Photograph or scan everything at consistent size and light. Reviewers read for judgement, so the reasoning matters more than the drawings.
days.minimum: Lay out the brief page and the thumbnail page. Ten minutes.
days.question: Can a stranger tell from page three why you killed the other two?

days.title: Project 1 — the rest of the pages
days.full: Then pages five to ten: refinement, orthographic views, the final rendering, and one page on what you would do differently. Keep the grid and the type consistent across every page — you are not designing a layout yet, you are being disciplined about one.
days.minimum: Lay out the rendering page. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which page are you including because it is good, and which to fill space?

days.title: Project 1, finished
days.full: No new material. Put the document together and read it once, end to end, as though someone else made it. Write three sentences in the notes: what the project proves you can do, what it exposes, and what you would cut if you had to get it to six pages.
days.minimum: Read it through and write the three sentences. Ten minutes.
days.question: What does it expose?

days.title: The benchmark object, halfway
days.full: The second redraw, and the halfway mark. Find the object from Day 1. Same conditions: fifteen minutes, cold, no construction, no reference. Photograph it. Then lay Day 1, Day 90 and Day 180 in a row — three specimens of the same thing, six months apart — and leave them out where you will walk past them.
days.minimum: Fifteen minutes on the object, photographed. The row of three can wait until tomorrow.
days.question: Halfway. Which of the three would you show someone, and which would you hide?

days.title: Structured observation
days.full: Project 4 phase opens away from the desk. Pick one public context where people use something — a bus stop, a supermarket self-checkout, a coffee shop counter, a hardware shop. Watch for forty-five minutes and sketch what actually happens, not what should. Count things. Note workarounds. Do not talk to anyone today. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Twenty-five minutes of watching, with three things sketched and one thing counted.
days.question: What did people do that the designer clearly did not expect?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Phase 4 has started and it does not look like the last three.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: The same place, a different lens
days.full: Go back to the same context for twenty minutes, watching one thing only: hands. What do people touch, how do they hold it, what do they put down and pick up again. Sketch six hands doing six things. Same place, one variable.
days.minimum: Fifteen minutes, three hands sketched.
days.question: What is being held that was never designed to be held?

days.title: One activity, as a sequence
days.full: Pick one person's activity from your observations and draw it as a strip of eight frames, start to finish, like a storyboard. No words in the frames. Where a step repeats, draw it repeating.
days.minimum: Draw four frames of the sequence. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: Which frame is the one everybody would skip if they could?

days.title: Two methods, properly
days.full: Read two or three methods from Universal Methods of Design — start with the observational and interview ones. Twenty minutes, pen down. Pick one you will actually use this week and write its name in the notes.
days.minimum: Ten minutes. Name one method you will use.
days.question: Which method are you avoiding because it means talking to strangers?

days.title: The first interview
days.full: Write six questions, none of which can be answered yes or no, and none of which mention your idea. Then interview one real person for fifteen minutes about the activity you observed. Write down what they said, not what you concluded.
days.minimum: Write the six questions. Interview nobody today.
days.question: Which of your six questions was really you hoping for a particular answer?

days.title: Interviews two and three
days.full: Two more people, same six questions, fifteen minutes each. Resist improving the questions between interviews — you want the same instrument three times. Note where the three answers diverge.
days.minimum: One more interview, ten minutes.
days.question: Where did three people disagree, and is the disagreement the interesting part?

days.title: Lay the research out
days.full: Light week. Nothing new until day 195. Put every observation sketch, count and interview note on one surface. Do not analyse, do not cluster, do not conclude. Just get it all visible and photograph it. Short block.
days.minimum: Lay it out and photograph it. Ten minutes.
days.question: What is there more of than you remembered collecting?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. The research sits and marinates.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Reread your own notes
days.full: Light week. Read your interview notes again, three days later, as though someone else wrote them. Underline anything that surprises you now. Nothing new.
days.minimum: Read them once. Underline three things. Five minutes.
days.question: What reads differently now that you have forgotten saying it?

days.title: Redraw an observation
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then take your roughest observation sketch and draw it again properly, from memory and notes. Five weeks of rendering should show up here without you trying.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Did drawing it again tell you something the first sketch did not?

days.title: Rewatch something on process
days.full: Light week. Twenty minutes of Core77 or IDSA case-study material — a project written up start to finish. Watch or read it as a shape rather than for content: how much space goes to research, how much to making.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of it.
days.question: How much of a published case study is the part you are doing right now?

days.title: What you noticed and did not write down
days.full: Light week. Sit with the research for ten minutes and write down three things you remember noticing but never recorded. These are usually the useful ones, which is an uncomfortable fact about note-taking.
days.minimum: Write down one thing you never recorded. Five minutes.
days.question: Why did you not write those down at the time?

days.title: Just the warm-up
days.full: Light week, last day. The warm-up and nothing else: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Twenty-eight weeks in and it is still the first thing you do.
