days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Has the warm-up become automatic, or are you still thinking about it?

days.title: Interviews four and five
days.full: Two final interviews, same six questions. Then transcribe all five properly — actual words, not summaries. Transcription is tedious and it is where the insight usually arrives, because you hear the second half of sentences you talked over. Fill the block.
days.minimum: One interview, then transcribe the best five minutes of it. Thirty minutes.
days.question: What did someone say that you talked over at the time?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Journey mapping
days.full: Draw the whole activity as a journey: stages across, and underneath each one what the person does, what they feel, and what goes wrong. Use the five interviews, not your imagination. One large sheet.
days.minimum: Draw the stages across the top and the actions underneath. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: Where on the map is the worst moment, and is it where you assumed?

days.title: The low point
days.full: Take the worst moment on the map and expand it into its own map — the thirty seconds around it, frame by frame. Most products get designed for the average moment. The interesting design lives in the worst one.
days.minimum: Draw the worst moment as four frames. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: Is the low point a design problem, or just life?

days.title: Clustering
days.full: Write every observation and quote onto its own scrap of paper — forty minimum — then move them into groups without naming the groups first. Name them only after they have stopped moving. Photograph the layout before you write any names.
days.minimum: Twenty scraps, clustered, unnamed. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: Which scrap refused to join a group?

days.title: Synthesis methods
days.full: Read two or three synthesis methods from Universal Methods of Design. Twenty minutes, pen down. You have just done clustering by instinct — read how it is supposed to go and note where you cut a corner.
days.minimum: Ten minutes. Name the corner you cut.
days.question: Which corner did you cut, and did it matter?

days.title: The point-of-view statement
days.full: No new material. Reframe everything into one sentence: a specific person needs a way to do a specific thing, because of a specific insight. Write eight versions. Delete the six that could describe anybody. The last two are your brief.
days.minimum: Write four versions of the sentence. Ten minutes.
days.question: Could your statement have been written before you did any of this research?

days.title: The hundred begins
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the ideation week starts: one hundred concept sketches by day 209. Today is for volume, not quality — get to twenty-five. Thumbnail size, no rendering, one idea per box, and number every single one. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then twelve thumbnails, numbered. Thirty minutes.
days.question: At which number did you stop having ideas and start having variations?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. The hundred can wait a day.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Analogy
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then fifteen more by analogy: what else in the world solves a structurally similar problem. A stapler and a stapler-shaped problem. Look at nature, at other industries, at things much bigger and much smaller than yours.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then eight sketches by analogy. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which analogy is a genuine structural match and which is just a shape you liked?

days.title: Forced connection
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then fifteen more by forced connection: open a dictionary or look around the room, take a random object, and make your concept borrow something from it. Most will be nonsense. Two will not be.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then eight forced connections. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which nonsense one would you secretly like to keep?

days.title: Ideation, watched
days.full: Twenty minutes of ideation and concept sketching material, drawing along. Watch how fast the sketches are and how little is committed to any one of them.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, drawing along.
days.question: How long does a concept sketch get before he moves on?

days.title: Constraint inversion
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then twenty more by inverting a constraint. Take something everyone assumes — it must be handheld, it must be one piece, it must be powered — and remove it. Draw what is left. The point is not that these are buildable.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then ten inversions. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which assumption was hardest to let go of?

days.title: The hundredth
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then get to one hundred. Whatever is left, draw it today. The last fifteen are the whole point of the first eighty-five, and you will not believe that until you see them.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then ten more, whatever they are. Ten minutes.
days.question: Are the last fifteen better, or just stranger?

days.title: One hundred, spread out
days.full: Lay all one hundred out at once and photograph them as a single grid. This is one of the best-looking things you will make all year and it took a week. Then, without deciding anything, mark every sketch you would be willing to show someone. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Lay them out, photograph the grid, mark ten. Thirty minutes.
days.question: How many of the hundred would you show someone, honestly?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. One hundred sketches exist that did not exist last week.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: A matrix, built honestly
days.full: No new sketching. Write the five criteria that actually matter for this brief — derived from the point-of-view statement, not invented now. Then score your ten marked concepts against them. Build the matrix before you look at which one wins.
days.minimum: Write the five criteria. Score three concepts. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: Did you write the criteria to fit the concept you already liked?

days.title: Killing your favourite
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then take the concept you most want to win and write down the three strongest arguments against it. If you cannot find three, you do not understand it yet. Then draw the two that beat it on the matrix, properly, at size.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then write the three arguments against your favourite. Ten minutes.
days.question: Did your favourite survive its own three arguments?

days.title: The Design of Everyday Things
days.full: Read Norman for twenty minutes, pen down. This is background reading for the whole phase rather than a one-sitting book — start it now and keep it going. Three sentences in the notes on one thing in your own concepts that fails his test.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: Which of your hundred concepts would Norman say cannot be understood on sight?

days.title: Three survivors
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw the three surviving concepts properly — three views each, at size, with real proportion. This is the first time this week that a drawing has had to be good rather than fast.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one survivor at two views. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which survivor got worse when you drew it large?

days.title: Defending the choice
days.full: No new material. Write half a page in the notes arguing for one concept over the other two, as though to someone who preferred a different one. Then write the strongest paragraph you can against your own choice. Reviewers read for judgement, and this is what judgement looks like written down.
days.minimum: Write the argument for. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is your argument about the concept, or about how much work you already put into it?

days.title: Rhino — Level 1 begins
days.full: CAD starts. Open McNeel's Level 1 guide and work it from the beginning, in order, doing every exercise rather than reading them. Do not skip to the thing you want to model. Your engineering background will make the first hours feel slow and the later ones fast. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Thirty minutes in the Level 1 guide, exercises done rather than read.
days.question: What does Rhino call something that you know by a different name?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Curves
days.full: Level 1 continued: point editing, curve tools, control points versus edit points. Everything downstream is made of curves, so a bad curve today is a bad surface on day 230.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes on curve tools.
days.question: How few control points can describe the curve you want?

days.title: Curve quality
days.full: Level 1 continued, plus the thing the guide treats lightly: curvature graphs. Turn them on and leave them on. A curve that looks right and graphs badly will surface badly, and you will not see why until it is too late.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes with the curvature graph on.
days.question: Does a curve that looks right ever graph well?

days.title: Draw it before you model it
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then, on paper, draw the object you intend to model next week: three views, a section, and the key radii marked. Modelling without drawing first is the trap engineers fall into hardest, because the software will happily let you design by accident.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two views and one section. Ten minutes.
days.question: What did drawing it first tell you that you would have discovered three hours into the model?

days.title: Surfaces from curves
days.full: Level 1 continued: surfaces from curves, extrusions, revolves, planar surfaces. Build each one twice — once as the guide says, once your own way — and compare.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes on surface tools.
days.question: Which surface tool are you overusing because it always works?

days.title: The same form, both ways
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then take a simple form, model it in twenty minutes, and draw it by hand in twenty minutes. Put a screenshot next to the drawing. They will be good at different things and it is worth knowing which is which before Project 2.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then draw the form by hand only. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which one communicates the idea faster, and which one proves it works?

days.title: Rhino — Level 1 finished
days.full: Finish Level 1. Then, without the guide open, model one object from your desk from scratch, measured with a ruler. It will take longer than you expect and that is the actual test. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Thirty minutes finishing Level 1 exercises.
days.question: Where did you get stuck, and was it the software or the geometry?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: A construction drawing for the model
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then prepare properly for Level 2: take your chosen Project 1 or ideation form and draw it as a construction document — orthographic views to scale, sections at three stations, radii called out. This is what you will model from.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one orthographic view with radii marked. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which dimension have you been avoiding deciding?

days.title: Lofts and sweeps
days.full: Level 2, surfacing: lofts, sweeps with one and two rails, networks. These are where a model starts looking like a product rather than an assembly of primitives. Build the same shape three ways and look at the isocurves.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes on lofts and sweeps.
days.question: Which of the three builds has the cleanest isocurves, and is it the one that was easiest?

days.title: Blends and fillets
days.full: Level 2 continued: fillets, blends, variable radius. This is Phase 2's corner treatment fortnight in software, and you will find the software is worse at it than your hand was. Find where the fillet fails and understand why.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes on fillets and blends.
days.question: Where does the fillet fail, and is it the radius or the surfaces underneath it?

days.title: The Level 2 guide, read
days.full: Read rather than click: twenty minutes of McNeel's Level 2 material on surfacing strategy. You have been building by trial and error for a week — read it as a correction. Three sentences in the notes on one habit you will drop.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. Name one habit to drop.
days.question: Which habit are you dropping, and why did you form it?

days.title: SubD for organic forms
days.full: SubD: the tool for the compound-curved forms you drew in Phase 2. Start from a box, subdivide, pull. It is closer to foam modelling than to engineering CAD, which is the point.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes in SubD from a box.
days.question: Does SubD feel more like drawing or more like modelling?

days.title: Your own drawing, modelled
days.full: The point of the whole block: take the construction drawing from day 225 and model it properly in Rhino. Your own form, your own decisions, to your own dimensions. Expect the drawing to have been wrong in at least two places. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Thirty minutes on the model. Stop wherever you get to.
days.question: Where was the drawing wrong, and would you have noticed on paper?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: KeyShot — materials
days.full: Import the Rhino model and start with materials only, in a flat grey scene. Assign a plastic, a metal, a rubber. You spent a fortnight in Phase 3 learning what these look like by hand, so you already know when the software is lying.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes assigning three materials.
days.question: Does the software's plastic look like the plastic you drew on day 131?

days.title: HDRI lighting
days.full: Lighting: swap HDRIs and watch the same model change character completely. Then build one deliberately — a key, a fill, and something for the edge. This is day 121 again, in a different tool.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes, three HDRIs compared.
days.question: Where is the light coming from, and did you decide or did the preset?

days.title: Plan the shot
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then thumbnail the render before you make it: six compositions on paper, deciding angle, crop, and where the eye should land. Rendering without composing first is how you end up with a grey object floating in the middle of a square.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then three composition thumbnails. Ten minutes.
days.question: Where do you want the eye to land, and what is putting it there?

days.title: KeyShot, watched
days.full: Twenty minutes of KeyShot's own learning material on studio setups and camera framing, working along. Watch the camera settings specifically — focal length does more for a product shot than any material setting.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of it.
days.question: What focal length is he using, and what would a different one do to the object?

days.title: Studio and camera
days.full: Build one studio setup you would use again: backdrop, lighting, camera, and a saved file you can drop future models into. Then frame the model three ways using your day 234 thumbnails.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes, one saved studio setup.
days.question: Which of the three framings makes the object look most expensive, and why that one?

days.title: A finished render, and a turntable
days.full: Render one hero image properly and one turntable animation of your own model. Then put the render next to the hand rendering from Project 1 and look at what each does better. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Thirty minutes, one hero render at low resolution.
days.question: Which is more convincing, and which is more yours?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Project 2 — a real need
days.full: Project 2 begins, and unlike Project 1 the need has to be observed rather than invented. Go back out with the day 181 method and watch a different context for thirty minutes. You are looking for a problem you can hold in your hand, not a system.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes watching. Three things sketched.
days.question: Is this a problem, or is it just something you would enjoy designing?

days.title: Phase 4, looked at properly
days.full: No new material. Write the Project 2 brief as a point-of-view statement using the day 201 format. Then look back at the phase: lay out the hundred sketches, the journey map, and the Rhino model together and write in the notes which of the three you would show an admissions reviewer first.
days.minimum: Write the Project 2 point-of-view statement. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the three would you show first, and is that the same as which you are proudest of?

days.title: Model-making, watched
days.full: Light week, and Phase 5 needs things you do not own yet. Spend twenty minutes on Core77 model-making how-tos, and while you watch, write the shopping list: blue foam, foam core, a fresh scalpel, sandpaper from 80 to 400, spot putty, primer. Order it today so it arrives before day 248.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, and write the shopping list.
days.question: What are they using that costs almost nothing, and what actually needs buying?

days.title: Lay out Phase 4
days.full: Light week. Put the hundred sketches, the journey map, the Rhino screenshots and the KeyShot render out together. Eight months of this and the work has started to look like a body of work rather than a pile of exercises.
days.minimum: Lay it out. Five minutes.
days.question: Which of them looks least like a student made it?

days.title: A place to make a mess
days.full: Light week. Set up somewhere you can generate dust: a surface you do not mind ruining, a way to get air moving, a dust mask that actually seals, and somewhere to put sharp things. Foam dust is the main hazard of this phase and it gets everywhere.
days.minimum: Clear the surface and find the mask. Ten minutes.
days.question: Where in your home can you make a genuine mess without it becoming a negotiation?

days.title: One block of foam, no goal
days.full: Light week, short block. Take one piece of blue foam and cut, rasp and sand it into nothing in particular. No object, no reference, no plan. You are learning what the material does before you ask it to do something.
days.minimum: Fifteen minutes with the foam, then stop.
days.question: How fast does it cut, and how fast does it break?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Warm-up, and one unfinished thing
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then redraw one drawing from Phase 4 that you never finished properly. Thirty-five weeks in and the warm-up has not changed once.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Do your ellipses look different from day 15, or only faster?

days.title: Plan the phase
days.full: Light week, last day. Read the contents of Hallgrimsson and decide which three techniques you will actually use on Project 2. You cannot learn all of them in twelve days, so choose now rather than drifting.
days.minimum: Pick three techniques. Five minutes.
days.question: Which technique are you choosing because it suits the object, and which because it looks impressive?

days.title: Foam core, flat
days.full: Foam core first because it is cheap and unforgiving. Cut six panels dead square with a fresh blade — one pass to score, one to cut, never sawing. Then cut six more at forty-five degrees for mitred corners. A blunt blade tears foam core and there is no recovering it.
days.minimum: Cut three square panels cleanly. Ten minutes.
days.question: How many cuts before the blade stops being sharp enough?

days.title: Materials and tools
days.full: Read Hallgrimsson on materials and tools. Twenty minutes, pen down. You have made two cuts and you already have opinions — read it as a correction. Three sentences in the notes on a tool you do not have and probably need.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. Name one tool you are missing.
days.question: What is the cheapest tool that would have saved you the most time so far?

days.title: Foam core, joined
days.full: Then boxes: mitred corners, butt joints, and one with an internal frame. Three volumes, each one dimensioned from a drawing rather than made up as you go. Check them for square when you finish, and note which joint failed.
days.minimum: Build one box with mitred corners. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which joint went out of square, and was it the cut or the glue?

days.title: Something full size
days.full: Build a full-scale foam core mockup of a real object you own — same dimensions, no detail, no finish. Then put it next to the real thing. Scale drawings lie to you constantly and this is the fastest way to find out how. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Build the main volume at full size. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Is it the size you expected, and if not, which dimension was your drawing wrong about?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Blue foam, roughed out
days.full: Blue foam now. Draw the silhouette on two faces of the block, then cut to the lines with a saw and rasp it down. Stay outside the line — every bit you remove is gone. This is subtractive thinking, which is the opposite of everything you did in CAD.
days.minimum: Rough out one form to its silhouette. Ten minutes.
days.question: How much did you leave outside the line, and was it enough?

days.title: Eighty to four hundred
days.full: Sanding properly: 80 to shape, 120 to fair, 240 to smooth, 400 to finish. Do the whole ladder on one form and skip a grit on another. The skipped one will show scratches under primer and you should see that happen once rather than be told.
days.minimum: Take one form from 80 to 240. Ten minutes.
days.question: Can you see the grit you skipped, and at what stage did it become visible?

days.title: Templates before you carve
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw the templates for the next carve: the silhouette from two directions and three section profiles, cut out of card so you can offer them up to the foam as you work. Carving without templates is how you end up with a symmetrical object that is not symmetrical.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one silhouette template drawn and cut. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which section is the one that will tell you the form has gone wrong?

days.title: Filler
days.full: Bondo for the big errors, spot putty for the small ones. Mix small, work fast, and put on more than you need. Then sand it back. Filler is not cheating — appearance models are mostly filler and everyone pretends otherwise.
days.minimum: Fill one low spot and sand it back. Ten minutes.
days.question: How many rounds of fill and sand before the surface stops revealing new low spots?

days.title: Draw what you actually carved
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw the form you have made, from three angles, measuring rather than remembering. Comparing this drawing to the day 255 templates will tell you exactly where the carve drifted. Most drift happens on the face you cannot see while you work.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the form from one angle, measured. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which face drifted, and is it the one you were not looking at?

days.title: Primer and paint
days.full: Primer first — thin coats, and the first one is only there to show you every flaw you missed. Sand back, prime again, then colour. Wet sand between coats. Fill the block, and stop before you have added one coat too many.
days.minimum: Two thin coats of primer with a sand between. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: What did the primer reveal that you were sure was flat?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Works-like, and ugly
days.full: A works-like model has one job: proving the mechanism. No finish, no proportion, no shame. Build one for the moving or working part of Project 2 out of card, tape and whatever is in the drawer. Half an hour, deliberately ugly.
days.minimum: Build the mechanism roughly. Ten minutes.
days.question: Does it work, and if not, is that a geometry problem or a material one?

days.title: Looks-like, and useless
days.full: Now the opposite: the same idea as an appearance model that does nothing at all. Correct proportion, correct surfaces, no function. Keeping these two separate is the single most useful habit in this phase — combining them too early kills both.
days.minimum: Block out the appearance model in foam. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the two taught you more, and which would you show someone?

days.title: What each model is for
days.full: Read Hallgrimsson on prototyping strategy — which kind of model answers which kind of question. Twenty minutes, pen down. Then write in the notes the one question your Project 2 model needs to answer.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. Write the one question.
days.question: What question is your model actually answering, and did you choose it or inherit it?

days.title: Round one, in the hand
days.full: Build the Project 2 form at full size, roughly, and hold it. Not look at it — hold it. Where does it press, where do your fingers go without being told, what do you want to move. Schools want to see the ugly middle, so photograph it exactly as it is.
days.minimum: Build it roughly and hold it for five minutes. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: What did your hand do that you did not design for?

days.title: Draw round one, and its failures
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw the model you built yesterday and annotate every failure directly on the drawing — too thick here, edge digs in there, thumb has nowhere to go. Ten annotations minimum. Annotated drawings of failures are portfolio material; clean renderings of successes are everywhere.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the model drawn with five annotations. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which failure did you notice only once you had to draw it?

days.title: Round two
days.full: Rebuild it, fixing the three worst problems from round one and deliberately leaving the others. Changing one thing at a time is slow; changing everything at once means you learn nothing. Fill the block, then hold it again.
days.minimum: Rebuild the worst part only. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Did fixing the worst problem create a new one?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Round two, tested properly
days.full: Give it to two other people without explaining it and watch what they do. Do not help. Do not defend it. Write down what they did in the first ten seconds, which is the only part that is not politeness.
days.minimum: Hand it to one person and watch. Ten minutes.
days.question: What did they do in the first ten seconds?

days.title: Round three, on paper first
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw round three before building it, incorporating everything from the two tests. Section drawings, wall thicknesses, the bit that has to flex. This is the drawing that proves you are designing rather than whittling.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one section drawing for round three. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is round three a change of detail or a change of idea?

days.title: Round three
days.full: Build it. This is the form that goes into CMF and photography, so take the sanding to 400 and fill what needs filling. Three rounds is the minimum a reviewer wants to see and you now have them.
days.minimum: Build the main form. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: Is round three better, or just more finished?

days.title: The benchmark object, nine months on
days.full: The fourth redraw. Find the object from Day 1. Same conditions: fifteen minutes, cold, no construction, no reference, no technique you would not have had in January. Photograph it, then put all four in a row — Day 1, 90, 180, 270. One redraw left.
days.minimum: Fifteen minutes on the object, photographed.
days.question: Four drawings of one object. Which pair shows the biggest jump?

days.title: Round three, finished
days.full: Finish the model: final filler, final sanding, primer. Leave it unpainted — colour is next fortnight's decision and painting it now would commit you before you have made it.
days.minimum: Prime it. Ten minutes.
days.question: Under primer, is the form as good as you thought it was under filler?

days.title: Three rounds, together
days.full: Line the three rounds up in order and photograph them properly — same light, same background, same distance. This single image does more in a portfolio than any rendering, because it shows process rather than claiming it. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Line them up and photograph them. Twenty minutes.
days.question: Looking at the three together, which round was the real decision?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Colour, chosen rather than picked
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then five colourways for the Project 2 form, each one justified in a sentence: who it is for, where it lives, what it is signalling. Then one deliberately wrong colourway so you can see what wrong looks like next to right.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two colourways with their sentences. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the five is the safe one, and would you regret it in a portfolio?

days.title: A board of real things
days.full: Gather physical samples — offcuts, swatches, a piece of anodised metal from something broken, fabric, a textured plastic. Stick them to a board. Photographs of materials lie about texture and weight, which is the entire reason material boards are physical.
days.minimum: Gather four physical samples. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which sample felt different from how it looked?

days.title: One form, three CMF directions
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the same form rendered three times under three complete CMF directions — colour, material and finish all moving together rather than colour alone. Clinical, warm, and rugged. Same object, three markets.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the form in one CMF direction. Ten minutes.
days.question: Does changing the material change who the object is for more than colour does?

days.title: Why a material reads that way
days.full: Read Ashby and Johnson on material perception. Twenty minutes, pen down. This is the difference between choosing a finish because it looks good and choosing it because of what it says. Three sentences in the notes.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: What does the material you chose say, and is that what you meant it to say?

days.title: Three finishes, one block
days.full: Paint one foam block three ways: gloss, matte, and something textured — stipple, spatter, or a coarse primer left unsanded. Then hold all three under the same light. You have been drawing these finishes since day 131 and this is the first time you can feel them.
days.minimum: Paint one block in two finishes. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which finish photographs best, and is that the same as which feels best?

days.title: The CMF board
days.full: Build the real thing for Project 2: the chosen colourway, physical material samples, finish samples, and a line of text saying why. One board, photographable, portfolio quality. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Assemble the board with the colour and two samples. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Can someone understand the decision from the board alone, with you not in the room?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Specifying it
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then write the finish specification as though handing it to a factory: each surface, its material, its finish, its texture, and where the transitions happen, drawn on an exploded view. Your engineering background makes this the easiest day of the fortnight and it is the one most design students cannot do.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then specify three surfaces on a drawing. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which surface did you not have an answer for?

days.title: What the finish costs
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then cost your three CMF directions roughly — soft-touch coating, in-mould texture, secondary operations, extra tooling. A soft-touch coating is a business decision as much as an aesthetic one, and knowing that is most of what separates a designer from a stylist.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then rank the three by cost with one line of reasoning each. Ten minutes.
days.question: Would you still choose it if it added fifteen per cent to the unit cost?

days.title: The CMF, decided
days.full: No new material. Choose the final CMF for Project 2 and write half a page defending it against the other two — user, context, cost, and what it signals. Then write the strongest sentence you can against your own choice.
days.minimum: Choose it and write three sentences. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is the sentence against your choice one you can live with?

days.title: Lay out Phase 5
days.full: Light week. Nothing new until day 291. Put the foam core mockup, the three prototype rounds, the finish samples and the CMF board on one surface. This is the first phase where the work is three-dimensional and it takes up a startling amount of room.
days.minimum: Lay it out and photograph it. Five minutes.
days.question: Does the physical work look better or worse than the drawings of it?

days.title: Warm-up, and a failure drawn properly
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then redraw one of the annotated failure drawings from day 264 — same model, same annotations, drawn properly this time. It is going in the portfolio, so it should not look like a note to yourself.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Can you make a drawing of a failure look deliberate without making it look dishonest?

days.title: Sand something properly
days.full: Light week, short block. Take an old model — round one, the first foam block, anything — and sand it to 400 with no goal beyond the surface. Repetitive, quiet, and it is the skill that most separates a good appearance model from a student one.
days.minimum: Fifteen minutes of sanding, then stop.
days.question: At which grit does it stop feeling like work?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Draw a model you made
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then draw one of your own physical models from three angles, from life. You spent Phase 2 drawing other people's objects; this is the first time the object on the table is yours.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is your own object harder to draw honestly?

days.title: Reread the test notes
days.full: Light week. Read what you wrote when you handed round two to two other people. Three weeks later, decide whether you actually acted on it or just recorded it.
days.minimum: Read the notes. Five minutes.
days.question: Did you act on what they did, or on what you already wanted to do?

days.title: Rewatch a model-making video
days.full: Light week, last day. Rewatch something from day 241, now that you have spent six weeks with foam and filler. Photography starts tomorrow.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of it.
days.question: What looked like magic in week one and looks like patience now?

days.title: A backdrop that disappears
days.full: Build a seamless: a sheet of white or mid-grey card curved from vertical to horizontal with no visible join, big enough that the model never reaches its edges. Two clamps and a wall will do it. The join is the thing that gives away an amateur product shot.
days.minimum: Build the sweep and put the model on it. Ten minutes.
days.question: Can you see where the backdrop stops being vertical?

days.title: The shot list
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw the six frames you need before you shoot any of them: hero three-quarter, straight-on front, detail of the best transition, the object in a hand, the three rounds together, and the CMF board. Drawing the shot list first is the difference between a set and a pile.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then draw three of the six frames. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the six is the one image, if you only got one?

days.title: One light, six frames
days.full: Shoot the whole set with a single light source and something white to bounce with — a sheet of paper is enough. Phone camera, locked exposure, no flash, no filters. Shoot each frame five times and move the light between takes. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Shoot the hero frame properly, five takes. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Where is your light, and would you have lit a drawing of this the same way?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Levels, dust, consistency
days.full: Retouch the set: match the exposure and white balance across all six, remove dust and fingerprints, straighten what is crooked. Consistency across a set matters more than any single image being perfect — a reviewer reads six shots as one object, and a mismatched one reads as a different day.
days.minimum: Match the exposure across three images. Ten minutes.
days.question: Do the six look like they were shot in one session?

days.title: Twelve to fifteen pages, planned
days.full: Plan the Project 2 document as a sequence of pages on one sheet — thumbnails of spreads, not content. Research, insight, ideation, the three rounds, CMF, final. Decide the page count before you start filling pages, or it will become nineteen.
days.minimum: Thumbnail the first six spreads. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which section are you giving the most pages to, and does it deserve them?

days.title: Pages one to five
days.full: Build the first five pages: the observation, the interviews, the journey map, the point-of-view statement. This is the half of a portfolio that most career-changers skip and most admissions tutors look for first, because it is the part that cannot be faked with drawing skill.
days.minimum: Lay out the observation and journey map pages. Ten minutes.
days.question: Would a reviewer believe you actually left the house?

days.title: Pages six to ten
days.full: Ideation and prototyping: the sketches, the selection, the three rounds with their annotations, what each round changed and why. Show the round you got wrong at the same size as the one you got right.
days.minimum: Lay out the three-rounds page. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is the failed round shown at the same size as the successful one, and if not, why not?

days.title: Pages eleven to fifteen
days.full: CMF, the finished model, the photographed set, and one page on what you would do differently. Keep the grid identical to Project 1's document even though you now know more about layout — consistency across projects reads as intent.
days.minimum: Lay out the final model page. Ten minutes.
days.question: What would you do differently, said in one sentence a stranger would understand?

days.title: Phase 2 finished, Phase 5 reviewed
days.full: Read the document end to end as though someone else made it, then write in the notes: what Project 2 proves that Project 1 did not, and which single page you would delete. Then look at the whole phase — you have made physical objects this quarter, which is the thing that was missing from the first two hundred days. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Read it through and write the two answers. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: Which page would you delete?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Phase 6 starts tomorrow and it is the one that produces the thing you apply with.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Project 3 — the hard constraint
days.full: The project that should lead the portfolio. Higher ambition than Project 2: either a product with a system or service around it, or a genuinely hard constraint — a cost ceiling, a single material, an extreme user, a context with no power. Write the brief and the constraint, and make the constraint one that will actually hurt.
days.minimum: Write the brief and the constraint. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: Is your constraint one that changes the answer, or one you can design around?

days.title: Project 3 — research, compressed
days.full: One observation session and two interviews, today and tomorrow, using the Phase 4 methods at speed. Four weeks for the whole project means research is days rather than weeks, which is also what it will be in practice.
days.minimum: Thirty minutes of observation, sketched.
days.question: What can you learn in one session that you could not have guessed?

days.title: How a project gets told
days.full: Read two Core77 or IDSA project case studies end to end, twenty minutes, pen down — not for the products but for the structure. Count how many paragraphs go to the problem before anything is drawn. Three sentences in the notes.
days.minimum: Read one case study. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: How much of a good case study is finished work?

days.title: Project 3 — the statement
days.full: Write the point-of-view statement in the day 201 format, then eight variants, then delete the six that could describe any product. Pin the survivor somewhere you will see it for the next four weeks.
days.minimum: Write four variants. Ten minutes.
days.question: Does the statement contain the constraint, or has it quietly dropped it?

days.title: Project 3 — sixty thumbnails begin
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then start the divergence: sixty thumbnails by tomorrow evening. Use everything from day 204 to 207 — analogy, forced connection, constraint inversion. Number them all.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then fifteen thumbnails. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which technique is producing the strange ones this time?

days.title: Project 3 — sixty reached
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then finish the sixty, lay them out and photograph the grid. Mark the ten you would show. Then hand the constraint back to yourself: strike out every thumbnail that quietly ignores it. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then twenty more thumbnails. Thirty minutes.
days.question: How many of your favourites were ignoring the constraint?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Project 3 — three directions
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then three directions drawn properly at size, three views each, chosen for difference rather than quality. One of them should be the one that takes the constraint most literally.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one direction at two views. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which direction does the constraint the most honestly, and is it the ugliest?

days.title: Project 3 — the matrix
days.full: No new sketching. Criteria from the point-of-view statement, scored honestly, matrix built before you look at the winner. Then write three arguments against the one you want to win.
days.minimum: Write the criteria and score one direction. Ten minutes.
days.question: Did the matrix agree with you, and what did you do when it did not?

days.title: Project 3 — refinement
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then refine the survivor: proportion, stance, corner treatment, parting lines, the bits that have to come apart. Four angles and one section. Everything from Phase 2 is doing the work here.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the form from two angles. Ten minutes.
days.question: What have you changed since the thumbnail, and was it an improvement or a retreat?

days.title: Products that come with a system
days.full: Twenty minutes on a project where the object is only part of the answer — a service, a refill, a network, a business model. If Project 3 is the systems one, this is the reference; if it is the hard-constraint one, watch it anyway and note what the object alone could not do.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of it.
days.question: Where does the object stop and the system start?

days.title: Project 3 — orthographics
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then front, side, top, two sections and overall dimensions. This drawing is what you model from next week, so decide the numbers now rather than in the software.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then two views with dimensions. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which dimension are you still guessing at?

days.title: Project 3 — modelling begins
days.full: Into Rhino with the orthographics. Build the primary surfaces first and resist detailing anything. Six weeks since Level 2 and the first hour will be slow. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Thirty minutes, primary surfaces only.
days.question: What have you forgotten since day 230, and what stuck?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Project 3 — surfacing
days.full: Surfacing properly: lofts and sweeps for the main body, curvature graphs on, isocurves checked. A surface that is nearly right now is a fillet that fails on Thursday.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes on the main body surfaces.
days.question: Is the surface actually continuous, or does it only look continuous?

days.title: Project 3 — fillets and detail
days.full: Fillets, variable radii, parting lines, and the details that make it a manufactured object rather than a shape. Where the fillet fails, fix the surface underneath rather than reducing the radius.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes on fillets.
days.question: Did you reduce a radius to make the software happy?

days.title: Draw what you cannot model
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then draw by hand the parts the CAD is not carrying — how it is held, how it is opened, what happens in use, the bit of the system that is not an object. A portfolio of clean renders with no hand drawing in it reads as a CAD exercise.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then one drawing of it in use. Ten minutes.
days.question: What can your hand say about this object that the model cannot?

days.title: Project 3 — model finished
days.full: Finish the model to the level you need for rendering and for driving the physical build. Then export what you need for both. Stop detailing things nobody will see.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes finishing. Export one view.
days.question: What did you detail that will never be visible?

days.title: Project 3 — into foam
days.full: Print the orthographics at full size, make templates, and rough the form out of blue foam. The model exists digitally, so this is about proportion in the hand rather than discovery — but it will still be wrong somewhere.
days.minimum: Rough out the silhouette. Ten minutes.
days.question: Now that it is real size, what is wrong that the screen hid?

days.title: Project 3 — the appearance model
days.full: Carve, fill and sand to 400. This is the object that gets photographed and it is the one physical thing an admissions reviewer will wish they could pick up. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Carve and fill the main form. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Which surface are you avoiding because it is hard to sand?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Project 3 — filler and patience
days.full: Another round of filler and sanding, then primer. Then look at it under primer and decide honestly whether the form is right. It is still cheap to change today and expensive to change on Friday.
days.minimum: One round of fill and sand. Ten minutes.
days.question: Under primer, would you still choose this form?

days.title: Project 3 — the finish
days.full: Paint it in the CMF you specified, thin coats, wet sanding between. Do the finish you decided rather than the one that is easiest — the whole point of Phase 5 was to make that a real choice.
days.minimum: Two coats. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is this the finish you specified, or the one you had paint for?

days.title: Project 3 — CMF on paper
days.full: Warm-up: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses on varying minor axes. Then the CMF board for Project 3: colourway, materials, finishes, and one line on what each is signalling. Shorter than Project 2's because you know the format now.
days.minimum: Warm-up, then the colourway and two samples. Ten minutes.
days.question: What is this finish signalling that Project 2's was not?

days.title: Project 3 — the render, set up
days.full: Into KeyShot with the day 236 studio file. Materials to match the physical model, HDRI lighting decided rather than defaulted, camera framed from the thumbnails you will draw today.
days.minimum: Twenty minutes, materials and lighting.
days.question: Does the render match the object on your desk, and which one is lying?

days.title: Project 3 — the hero images
days.full: Render the set: one hero three-quarter, one straight-on, one detail, one exploded or sectioned. Match the framing to the photographs you will take of the physical model so the two sit together on a page.
days.minimum: Render the hero image at low resolution. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: Should the render and the photograph look the same, or deliberately different?

days.title: Project 3 — photographed
days.full: Shoot the physical model on the seamless with the single-light setup, matching the render's framing. Then shoot the process: the foam roughs, the templates, the primer stage. Process photographs are the ones you will wish you had taken. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Shoot the hero frame and one process shot. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Which process photograph did you nearly not bother taking?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Project 3 — what it proves
days.full: No new material. Put everything from Project 3 in one place: research, sixty thumbnails, three directions, the model, the object, the photographs. Write in the notes what this project proves that Projects 1 and 2 do not, in one sentence.
days.minimum: Lay it out and write the sentence. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is it a better project, or just a bigger one?

days.title: Three projects, side by side
days.full: Light week. Nothing new until day 338. Lay out all three projects together for the first time. This is the portfolio in raw form, and it is the last light week of the year.
days.minimum: Lay them out and photograph the spread. Five minutes.
days.question: Which project does something the other two do not?

days.title: Look at other people's portfolios
days.full: Light week. Twenty minutes of Core77 portfolio critiques or Design Awards entries, looking only at structure: how many projects, how many pages each, what comes first. Do not read your own work against theirs today.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of it.
days.question: How many projects does a good portfolio actually contain?

days.title: Sort everything, best to worst
days.full: Light week. Sort every drawing, model and render from the whole year into three piles: portfolio, maybe, no. Do it fast and do not agonise. The maybe pile is the interesting one.
days.minimum: Sort one project's work into three piles. Ten minutes.
days.question: What is in the maybe pile, and what would move it either way?

days.title: Warm-up, and something from the maybe pile
days.full: Light week. Warm-up, then redraw one thing from the maybe pile that is only in that pile because the drawing is weak. Forty-eight weeks of warm-up behind you.
days.minimum: The warm-up only: one page of straight lines, one page of ellipses. Ten minutes.
days.question: Is it a weak drawing or a weak idea?

days.title: Reshoot one bad photograph
days.full: Light week, short block. Find the photograph that is letting a good piece of work down and take it again properly. One image, as many attempts as it takes.
days.minimum: Reshoot it three times. Fifteen minutes.
days.question: What was wrong with the first one — the light, the framing, or the object?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Choose what goes in
days.full: Light week, last day of the last light week. Decide what the portfolio contains and in what order. Three projects and some supporting sketch work is a portfolio; five projects is a filing cabinet. Layout starts tomorrow.
days.minimum: Decide the order of the three projects. Ten minutes.
days.question: What are you including that you already know is weaker than the rest?

days.title: A grid, built once
days.full: Build one grid and commit to it for the whole document: columns, gutters, margins, baseline. Do it on paper first and then in InDesign. Every page for the rest of the year sits on this, so an hour here saves a week later.
days.minimum: Draw the grid on paper and set the margins. Ten minutes.
days.question: How many columns do you actually need, and are you adding more out of nerves?

days.title: The grid, applied
days.full: Take three finished pages from the Project 2 document and rebuild them on the new grid. Images snap to columns, captions sit on the baseline, nothing floats. The difference is not subtle and you should be slightly annoyed by how much better it looks.
days.minimum: Rebuild one page on the grid. Ten minutes.
days.question: What was the old layout hiding?

days.title: How a spread is supposed to work
days.full: Read Eissen and Steur, Product Design Presentation, on layout and page-level decisions. Twenty minutes, pen down. Three sentences in the notes on one thing you have been doing that the book would not.
days.minimum: Ten minutes of reading. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: What are you doing on every page that the book never does once?

days.title: Hierarchy
days.full: Three levels of type and no more: project title, section heading, body. One typeface, two weights, one size ratio. Then set one page with the hierarchy deliberately wrong so you can see what the reader does with their eye.
days.minimum: Set the three levels and apply them to one page. Ten minutes.
days.question: Where does your eye land first, and is that where you wanted it?

days.title: Project 1, laid out
days.full: Rebuild Project 1 on the grid, in full. It is the weakest of the three and it is going in anyway, because it shows a starting point and reviewers read a portfolio as a trajectory. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Lay out three spreads. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Does Project 1 look like the beginning of something, or like filler?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Pacing
days.full: Print every spread small and lay them in a row. A portfolio has rhythm: dense pages, then a full-bleed image, then white space. If every spread has the same density, a reviewer stops seeing any of them.
days.minimum: Print the spreads small and lay them out. Ten minutes.
days.question: Where does the document sag?

days.title: Sequencing
days.full: Order the images inside each project so a reviewer's eye lands where you want it, in the order you want. The first image of each project decides whether they read the rest, and it is almost never the hero render.
days.minimum: Choose and place the first image for each project. Ten minutes.
days.question: What is the first image of each project, and why that one?

days.title: InDesign, properly
days.full: Twenty minutes of Adobe's own InDesign tutorials, working along: master pages, paragraph styles, and placing images without distorting them. Free, and enough. Learn styles specifically — they are what makes a change on day 360 take one minute instead of two hours.
days.minimum: Ten minutes, and set up one paragraph style.
days.question: What are you doing by hand on every page that a style could do once?

days.title: Project 2, laid out
days.full: Rebuild Project 2 on the grid. It is the one with real research in it, so give the research the space it deserves rather than rushing to the model.
days.minimum: Lay out two spreads. Ten minutes.
days.question: Are you giving the research pages the same care as the rendering pages?

days.title: Project 3, laid out
days.full: Rebuild Project 3 on the grid, and lead with it. This project opens the portfolio, so its first spread is the most important page in the whole document.
days.minimum: Lay out the opening spread. Ten minutes.
days.question: Does the opening spread work with the text covered up?

days.title: The whole thing, once through
days.full: Assemble everything into one document and read it start to finish without fixing anything. Note what is wrong on a list rather than correcting as you go. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Assemble it and read it once. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: What is wrong that you would not have seen page by page?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. Fifteen days left.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: The spine
days.full: Write the structure once and use it three times: context, insight, exploration, the decision you made and why, outcome. The decision section is the one reviewers actually read, because it is the only part that shows judgement rather than effort.
days.minimum: Write the five headings and fill in the first for one project. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which of the five sections do you least want to write, and what does that tell you?

days.title: Project 1, written
days.full: Write Project 1's case study to the spine. Three hundred words, no more. Its job is to establish that you can complete a loop, and then get out of the way.
days.minimum: Write the context and insight paragraphs. Ten minutes.
days.question: Can you say what Project 1 taught you without apologising for it?

days.title: Project 2, written
days.full: Project 2's case study, five hundred words. This is the one where the research has to earn its pages — quote a real person, show the journey map, name the insight that changed the design.
days.minimum: Write the insight and decision paragraphs. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which sentence in it could only have been written by someone who did the research?

days.title: Worked examples
days.full: Read three Core77 Design Awards entries, twenty minutes, pen down — this time for the writing rather than the structure. Note how much is process and how much is claim. Three sentences in the notes.
days.minimum: Read one entry. One sentence in the notes.
days.question: How do they describe a decision without sounding either arrogant or apologetic?

days.title: Project 3, written
days.full: Project 3's case study, six hundred words, and it leads the portfolio. The constraint has to be in the first two sentences. If the reader does not understand what made this hard, everything that follows reads as decoration.
days.minimum: Write the opening two sentences and the decision paragraph. Ten minutes.
days.question: Do the first two sentences make it clear what was hard?

days.title: The dead ends, written in
days.full: Go back through all three case studies and put the dead ends back — the direction you killed, the prototype that failed, the thing you got wrong and fixed. Reviewers read for judgement, and a project with no visible wrong turns reads as either lucky or dishonest. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Add one dead end to one case study. Twenty minutes.
days.question: Which dead end are you most reluctant to include, and is that the most useful one?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: Read it as a stranger
days.full: No new material. Read all three case studies end to end as though you had never seen the projects. Mark every sentence that assumes knowledge a reader does not have, and every sentence that could be deleted without loss. There will be more of the second kind.
days.minimum: Read one case study and mark it up. Ten minutes.
days.question: How many sentences survived?

days.title: Cut the image set
days.full: Remove a third of the images. Every portfolio has a third too many, and the ones you cut are almost always the process shots you are attached to rather than the ones that explain something. Then check what the remaining set says on its own.
days.minimum: Cut five images. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which image did you keep for sentimental reasons?

days.title: Two versions
days.full: Export a PDF under the size limit schools usually impose, and build a stripped web version. Check the PDF on a phone — most first reads happen on a screen smaller than the one you designed on, and type that works at A3 disappears at six inches.
days.minimum: Export the PDF and open it on your phone. Ten minutes.
days.question: What falls apart at phone size?

days.title: Statement of purpose, first draft
days.full: Write the first draft badly and completely: why design, why now, why this school, what the engineering background gives you that a design undergraduate does not have. Do not edit while writing. Six hundred words.
days.minimum: Write two hundred words of it. Ten minutes.
days.question: What does an engineer bring to a studio that nobody in the room already has?

days.title: Statement of purpose, second draft
days.full: Cut it by a third and make every claim specific — not that you are rigorous, but the thing you did that was rigorous. Then read it aloud. Anything you would not say out loud to a person comes out.
days.minimum: Cut a hundred words and read it aloud. Ten minutes.
days.question: Which sentence did you not want to say out loud?

days.title: Against the actual requirements
days.full: Go to each target school's live admissions page and check your materials against what they actually ask for right now — image counts, word limits, file formats, deadlines. Requirements change and nothing in this app should be trusted over the page itself. Make a checklist per school and mark what is missing. Fill the block.
days.minimum: Check one school's requirements and list what is missing. Twenty-five minutes.
days.question: Which school's requirements does your portfolio not currently meet?

days.title: Rest
days.full: Nothing scheduled. One day left.
days.minimum: Nothing.

days.title: The benchmark object, one year on
days.full: The last day, and the last redraw. Find the object you drew on Day 1. Same conditions: fifteen minutes, cold, no construction, no reference. Photograph it. Then lay out all five — Day 1, 90, 180, 270, 365 — and look at them properly. This is the only evidence that matters and you made it one day at a time.
days.minimum: Fifteen minutes on the object, photographed. Then put the five in a row.
days.question: A year ago you could not draw it. What would you tell whoever picks up a pen on their own Day 1?
